But DHT is only one part of the story, and blocking it without understanding the rest can leave women frustrated. When we look at the whole picture first, the plan gets simpler and far more personal to you.

shortAnswer.text: DHT can miniaturize genetically sensitive follicles, causing hairs to become finer and shorter in a patterned area. A widening part, temple or hairline thinning, and loss of volume make DHT worth discussing, but they do not prove it works alone. body.toc: Do DHT Blockers Actually Stop Hair Loss
body.text: Do DHT Blockers Actually Stop Hair Loss

A widening part or temples that keep creeping back may well involve DHT. Before you buy another blocker, it is worth understanding why this hormone attacks follicles at all, and what actually changes the outcome.

body.toc: You Have Read The Ads And You Are Not Sure
body.text: You Have Read The Ads And You Are Not Sure
The part is wider than it was. The temples have crept back. Somewhere in the middle of researching it you started seeing DHT blockers everywhere, and the pitch always sounds the same.

body.toc: What DHT Actually Does To Your Follicles
body.text: What DHT Actually Does To Your Follicles

So the fair question is whether any of this is real or whether it is another bottle with good marketing. The science behind DHT is real. It is also relevant for a lot of Black women whose pattern gets read as something else entirely. What follows is the part underneath the hype.

body.toc: The Problem With Most DHT Blockers
body.text: The Problem With Most DHT Blockers
Think of DHT as a bully that only picks on certain follicles. Genetic sensitivity decides who it targets, which is why two people with similar hormone levels can have very different hair.
Answers Before Blockers

Where a follicle is sensitive, DHT attaches to it and the growth phase shortens with each cycle. The hair that comes back is thinner and shorter than the one before it. That is miniaturization, and left long enough the follicle stops producing hair altogether.

body.toc: When DHT Blockers Actually Make Sense
body.text: When DHT Blockers Actually Make Sense
Once testing confirms DHT sensitivity is the primary driver rather than a side character, there are three places blockers earn their spot.

body.toc: What a DHT pattern can look like
body.text: What a DHT pattern can look like

items: A part that continues to widen
Thinning at the temples or hairline
Loss of volume that styling products do not change
Finer, shorter hairs appearing in a patterned area

body.text: Those signs make DHT a reasonable question. They do not prove it is the only driver. Inflammation, nutrient issues, stress, and other hormonal changes can exist beside a DHT-sensitive pattern.
Why genetic sensitivity matters

DHT does not affect every follicle in the same way. The article's bully comparison is useful because the target matters: genetically sensitive follicles can gradually produce finer and shorter hairs, while other follicles may remain unchanged.

body.toc: Why a blocker can be only part of the plan
body.text: Why a blocker can be only part of the plan

A blocker is aimed at one pathway. It does not automatically settle scalp inflammation, replace missing nutrients, or explain a stress-related shed. If the plan ignores those parts of the picture, even a reasonable DHT strategy can feel disappointing.
The goal is not to block a hormone because it appears on a label. It is to know whether DHT is acting on your follicles and what else is happening beside it.

faq.q: What does DHT do to hair follicles?
faq.a: DHT can attach to genetically sensitive follicles and gradually miniaturize them. The hairs those follicles produce become finer and shorter, which can make the part, temples, crown, or overall volume look different over time.

faq.q: What signs make DHT worth discussing?
faq.a: A widening part, thinning at the temples or hairline, loss of volume, and finer hairs in a patterned area are clues discussed here. They are not proof that DHT is the only cause.

faq.q: Why might a DHT blocker not be enough?
faq.a: A blocker addresses one pathway. It does not automatically settle scalp inflammation, replace missing nutrients, or explain stress-related shedding. Those factors can overlap with a DHT-sensitive pattern and may need their own attention.

faq.q: How does Dr. Nina decide if DHT is central?
faq.a: She reviews the distribution, hair caliber at 200x, scalp condition, and health timeline. When those pieces agree, a DHT-focused step can be considered in context rather than chosen from marketing alone.
